sentences.text: It took most of the summer to work out, and the working out was not magical in the least.
It was mostly asking people awkward questions and being wrong.
The rules, as far as Ines ever established them, were these.
A moth would not go to just anyone.
You could carry one out in your cupped hands to a person and open your hands and it would sit there like a scrap of paper, entirely uninterested, and eventually walk back up your sleeve.
It had to be dusk.
Not dark, not evening — dusk, the twenty minutes when the streetlights are on but you can still see the colour of things.
And you had to be standing near where the person had been when they lost it.
That was the part that made it hard, because it meant working out who, which meant asking, and there is no good way to ask an adult whether they have recently mislaid a dream about a boat.
She got round it by asking about the pictures instead.

The woman at the bakery, when Ines described a grey sea seen from the back of a boat, stopped counting change and said, "My father had a boat like that," and then, "Why?" — and Ines said she had seen a painting, which was a lie, but only a small one.
She let the boat moth go outside the bakery at dusk on a Thursday.
It went in through the top window, which was open for the heat, and did not come out.
The man who fixed bicycles had lost the hallway with the green door.

She was almost sure before she asked him and completely sure afterwards, from the way he said "that was my grandmother's house" and then stopped talking and went back to truing the wheel he had been truing.
She let it go outside his shop the following evening.
He was still there, working late, and he did not see her do it.
She watched from across the road as the moth went in under the shutter.
He came out about a minute later and stood on the pavement, looking at nothing in particular, for quite a long time.
Then he went back in and got on with the wheel.
He never mentioned it to her, and she never mentioned it to him, and for about a year afterwards he did her brake cables for nothing and neither of them ever said why.
She did nineteen that summer.
Nineteen out of hundreds, and it took her from June to the middle of September, and she got four of them wrong and had to bring them home again.
At the end of it she went up the ladder one last night before school started, expecting — she was not sure what.
Some visible dent.
Some gap in the rafters where nineteen used to be.
The attic looked exactly the same.
"It always does," her uncle said, from the crate.

"That's not a reason not to." And he left the light on, the way it had always been left on, and they went down and shut the trapdoor, and the humming went on very quietly above them all night, the way it had for years, the way it presumably still does.
